core_message: Thirty-three Chilean miners survived 69 days trapped 700 m underground, and all came out alive one by one in a narrow capsule.
title: The Note That Came Up From 700 Metres Down
description:
On 5 August 2010, part of the San Jose copper-gold mine near Copiapo, in Chile's Atacama Desert, collapsed, trapping 33 miners about 700 metres underground and some 5 km from the entrance. For 17 days nobody knew whether they were alive; they rationed their emergency food, reportedly two spoonfuls of tuna every two days. On 22 August a drill probe broke through near their shelter and came back up with a note taped to it: "Estamos bien en el refugio los 33" ("We are well in the shelter, the 33"). Supplies went down narrow boreholes while the families waited in a tent camp they called Camp Hope. On 12 and 13 October, after 69 days, all 33 were winched up one at a time in the Fenix 2 capsule; the last out was shift foreman Luis Urzua.

Source: Wikipedia, 2010 Copiapo mining accident.

scenes.narration: In 2010, thirty-three men came up from seven hundred metres underground, one at a time, in a capsule barely wider than a man.
On the fifth of August, part of the San Jose mine in Chile's Atacama Desert collapsed, trapping thirty-three miners deep inside the mountain.

For seventeen days nobody knew if they were alive. They rationed tiny spoonfuls of tuna. Then a drill broke through near their shelter, and came back up with a note: we are well in the shelter, the thirty-three.
Their families set up a tent town at the mine called Camp Hope, while rescuers drilled a shaft wide enough for a capsule.
After sixty-nine days, all thirty-three came out alive. The last one up was their shift boss, Luis Urzua.
